title: What’s New in Hand Surgery
abstract: This update is principally intended to highlight important knowledge advances in hand and wrist surgery for the practicing orthopaedic surgeon. I apologize in advance for any unintentional oversights or omissions. Trigger Finger Trigger finger is considered a straightforward condition to manage, but recent studies have informed the treatment process. Corticosteroid injection is the mainstay of nonoperative treatment for trigger finger. Bookman et al. attempted to define the optimal dosing for corticosteroid injections1 by administering 5-mg, 10-mg, or 20-mg Kenalog (triamcinolone acetonide) doses. They found a dose-dependent response, with the highest dose (20 mg) yielding meaningfully better clinical effectiveness for pain, function, and relief from symptoms at 6 months than either of the lower doses. The timeline for symptom relief after corticosteroid injection has now been well characterized by Bitar et al.2. The primary aim of that study was to compare 2 techniques for corticosteroid injection. The symptom relief was similar between the 2 techniques, but the most interesting finding was the timing of symptom abatement, with pain relief at 9 to 11 days, improvement in stiffness at 11 to 15 days, and resolution of triggering at 20 to 21 days after injection. Trigger finger surgery is one of the most common procedures in hand surgery. Most surgeons consider this to be a straightforward procedure with a short recovery period. Dogma suggests that A0 fibers should be released along with the A1 pulley during surgical treatment of trigger finger. A novel study randomized patients intraoperatively to have initial release of exclusively A0 or A1, followed by intraoperative retesting for triggering3. The results showed that, after A0-only release, 47% of patients had complete resolution of symptoms and, after A1-only release, 46% of patients had complete resolution of symptoms. All patients had complete resolution after release of both A0 and A1 fibers. Recovery after trigger finger release may not be as straightforward as surgeons believe. Blazar et al.4 suggested that recovery may take up to 1 year. Patients reported visual analog scale (VAS) pain and the abbreviated version of the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) Questionnaire (QuickDASH) at baseline and 4 weeks, 6 weeks, and 3, 6, 9, and 12 months postoperatively. They also completed a nonvalidated 6-question Perceived Recovery Survey at the same intervals. The median self-reported full recovery was 6 months, and 4 of 50 patients had not yet reported a full recovery by 12 months. Furthermore, a retrospective review of 3,428 patients showed that 17% of patients experienced at least 1 complication after trigger finger release using the International Consortium for Health Outcome Measurement Complications in Hand and Wrist Conditions (ICHAW) tool, although most of the complications were minor5. Several independent risk factors for complications were identified, including administration of corticosteroid injection in the 3 months prior to the surgical procedure, in keeping with other recent studies6,7. These findings may help surgeons to better counsel patients with regard to recovery from trigger finger treatment. Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Carpal tunnel syndrome may be a harbinger of systemic medical problems. Recently, there has been renewed study of the association between amyloidosis and carpal tunnel syndrome8. Certain subtypes of amyloidosis are associated with fatal cardiomyopathy, and early identification may lead to treatment and prevention of cardiac manifestations. It has been unclear which patients benefit from screening at the time of carpal tunnel release. Gannon and Ward reported the results of implementation of an amyloidosis screening algorithm where patients who met certain criteria (men ≥50 years of age and women ≥60 years of age with bilateral or previous carpal tunnel release, with or without additional conditions associated with amyloidosis such as spinal stenosis or history of cardiac disease) were offered screening9. There were 156 patients screened, and 75 (48%) met the criteria for biopsy. Of the eligible patients who accepted a biopsy (62 of 75), 22.5% tested positive for amyloid. Men were much more likely to have a positive result (30%) than women (13%). Another study showed a high incidence of undiagnosed diabetes or prediabetes in patients with peripheral neuropathy (carpal tunnel syndrome or cubital tunnel syndrome)10. Patients from a hand surgery clinic were sent for glucose challenge testing if they met the American Diabetes Association criteria for testing in asymptomatic adults (age of >45 years with a body mass index of >24 kg/m2 and another risk factor such as physical inactivity, high-risk race or ethnic group, family history, cardiovascular disease, hypertension). Those who underwent glucose challenge testing were then divided into 3 groups by diagnosis: (1) trigger finger, (2) peripheral neuropathy, or (3) other hand diagnoses (control group). Of patients who presented with neuropathy, 51.3% were prediabetic and 12.8% were frankly diabetic on the glucose challenge testing. This rate was almost double that of the control group, in which only 27.3% of patients had prediabetes and 6.8% of patients had diabetes. These studies highlight the need for surgeons to be aware of and screen for occult, serious, treatable medical problems in patients presenting with carpal tunnel syndrome. Outcomes of carpal tunnel release in the face of severe carpal tunnel syndrome are favorable for recovery of function and decrease in symptoms11. When the abductor pollicis brevis (APB) is nonfunctional, palmaris longus opponensplasty (Camitz transfer) has historically been recommended. However, a recent study has suggested that there is recovery of the APB even when the patient has an absent APB-CMAP (compound muscle action potential) preoperatively12. The study reviewed the results of functional, symptomatic, and electrophysiologic testing in 136 patients with an absent preoperative APB-CMAP. Sixty-four hands had a Camitz transfer performed concurrently with carpal tunnel release, and 72 hands had carpal tunnel release only. At 1 year, recovery was similar in both groups for all domains, including APB-CMAP amplitude. Carpal tunnel syndrome occasionally presents in atypical fashion. Piñal reported on 35 hands in 22 patients over 8 years who presented with otherwise inexplicable hand allodynia and lack of active finger flexion13. Common additional symptoms included sleep disturbance, radiation of pain to the forearm and/or shoulder, and hand swelling. On examination, all had better passive than active finger flexion, but passive finger flexion was painful. Painful Tinel and Phalen tests and painful dysesthesias were universally present. After carpal tunnel release, pain and swelling resolved, DASH scores improved from a mean of 67 to 20, and the mean tip-to-palm distance decreased from 3.7 to 0.3 cm. Most patients were able to make a composite fist immediately after the procedure. This is an enlightening series for those who have encountered patients like this. Arthritis Wrist Arthritis The treatment of wrist arthritis due to carpal malalignment, scaphoid nonunion, or systemic arthropathy certainly falls within the purview of the general orthopaedic surgeon. Common salvage procedures include proximal row carpectomy and scaphoid excision with intercarpal arthrodesis, typically 4-corner arthrodesis between the capitate, hamate, lunate, and triquetrum. Proximal row carpectomy is associated with good intermediate-term results, with a low rate of conversion to total wrist arthrodesis of 5.3% in 1,070 patients at a mean of 6.5 years14. When midcarpal arthritis is present, scaphoid excision with intercarpal arthrodesis is preferred. Several studies were published in the preceding year comparing various constructs and techniques for scaphoid excision with intercarpal arthrodesis. The summary of this literature suggests that longitudinal column arthrodesis from the lunate to capitate and hamate to triquetrum is sufficient compared with 4-corner arthrodesis. Various methods of instrumentation for 2-corner arthrodesis achieved high rates of union, good patient-reported outcomes, and no clear advantage of 4-corner arthrodesis over 2-corner arthrodesis15–19. Other studies emphasized the importance of positioning the lunate appropriately on the capitate in terms of coverage and neutral longitudinal alignment for long-term wrist range of motion and pain relief20. Patients with very poor preoperative range of motion may actually gain range of motion after scaphoid excision with intercarpal arthrodesis. Ahmad et al. reported that patients with a preoperative mean arc of 47° improved to a mean arc of 65° at 8 months21. Hand Arthritis Attempts to define the optimal surgical management of thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) arthritis are ongoing. Beyond trapezial excision, it remains unclear which additional procedure, if any, is necessary or best, since complications and outcomes are similar among a wide variety of methods22–24. After trapezial excision, simply passing a nonabsorbable suture between the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) and abductor pollicis longus at the base of the thumb metacarpal showed good 12 to 14-year follow-up results with respect to pain, function, and strength, with a very low revision rate25. The mean tourniquet time was 22 minutes, and no special equipment or implants were used. A novel, alternative method of surgical treatment of thumb CMC arthritis has been explored recently with interesting results. CMC joint denervation has been described previously, but there are 2 recent studies examining short-term to intermediate-term results of denervation alone compared with trapeziectomy with suture suspensionplasty26 or trapeziectomy plus ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition (T+LRTI)27. Both studies showed similar results between groups, with improvement in pain and function, but dramatically quicker return to activities with denervation alone compared with a procedure involving trapeziectomy (3 weeks compared with 3 to 4 months). Both studies had <10% revision to T+LRTI at short-term follow-up of 1 to 2 years. Denervation may have a place in the surgical treatment of CMC arthritis, although longer-term studies are warranted. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint arthroplasty has been shown to have excellent long-term survival in the Norwegian Arthroplasty Register. Nearly 3,000 primary MCP joint arthroplasties (98.7% 1-component silicone prostheses and 1.3% 2-component metal prostheses) were reviewed. Implant survival was 89% at 10 years and 84% at 20 years28. Revision was more common in the right hand, in patients <60 years of age at the time of the index procedure, and in patients with inflammatory arthritis. The type of prosthesis (1-component silicone compared with 2-component metal) and the finger involved showed no difference in failure. It has been established that short-term outcomes for nonoperative management of osseous mallet injuries, even with joint subluxation, are no different from those with surgical treatment. Some have been reluctant to treat these injuries nonoperatively, citing the risk of posttraumatic arthritis. Slichter et al. reviewed 52 patients treated nonoperatively for an osseous mallet injury at mean follow-up of 12.1 years (range, 9.9 to 15.5 years)29. They compared radiographic changes and range of motion with the contralateral, control, distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint and evaluated patient-reported pain and function. Compared with the control DIP joint, 23% to 25% (depending on the classification used) of injured DIP joints had increased radiographic arthritis but did not show clinically meaningful decreased range of motion. The patient-reported outcome measures showed no clinically meaningful difference in pain or function. Trauma Distal Radial Fracture It is important to identify features of distal radial fracture stability and instability so the appropriate level of treatment may be rendered. The Cast-OFF trial group reported on pilot data showing the feasibility of merely 1 week of plaster immobilization followed by an elastic bandage in treating nondisplaced or minimally displaced (dorsal angulation of ≤10°, radial shortening/shift of ≤2 mm) fractures of the distal radius30. They found that there was no difference between groups in pain or function at multiple time periods up to 1 year, but the groups were small (20 patients each), and several patients crossed over from the treatment group (elastic bandage) to the control group (4 to 5 weeks of casting). Nevertheless, there were no cases of loss of alignment in the treatment group. In contrast, Schmidt et al. prospectively followed 165 patients who were 18 to 75 years of age (median, 57 years) with a distal radial fracture to identify risk factors for late displacement31. All patients treated initially with closed reduction were included if they had acceptable radiographic alignment 10 to 14 days after the injury. title: Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race; Rise of the Rocket Girls: The Women Who Propelled Us, from Missiles to the Moon to Mars
abstract: Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race, Margot Lee Shetterly, William Morrow, 2016, $27.99 (368 pp.). ISBN 978-0-06-236359-6 Buy at AmazonRise of the Rocket Girls: The Women Who Propelled Us, from Missiles to the Moon to Mars, Nathalia Holt, Little, Brown and Co, 2016, $27.00 (352 pp.). ISBN 978-0-316-33892-9 Buy at AmazonAt perhaps no other moment in US history would stories of the first female mathematicians and engineers at NASA resonate as they do following the 2016 presidential election. Both Nathalia Holt and Margot Lee Shetterly describe the lives of previously obscure women “computers” who worked for NASA during the earliest phases of America’s space program. Shetterly’s Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race tells the story of African American computers at the Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory in Hampton, Virginia. Holt’s book, Rise of the Rocket Girls: The Women Who Propelled Us, from Missiles to the Moon to Mars, focuses on women at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in southern California. Both books slant toward popular, nonacademic audiences; a film adaptation of Shetterly’s book receives nationwide release this month (Hidden Figures, 20th Century Fox, 2016).Shetterly and Holt are part of a growing contingent of journalists and historians seeking to peel back the veneer of existing institutional histories of NASA facilities and give insight into the lives of the hundreds of thousands of workers who propelled the space program from floundering rocket development to the Sea of Tranquility and beyond. Each author found inspiration for her work in personal experiences. Shetterly was inspired by her own life in the African American community around Hampton. Holt found her subject by a more unusual path; she learned about one of the JPL engineers while searching online for name ideas for her first child.Rise of the Rocket Girls and Hidden Figures offer moving glimpses into the growing pains of professional development for women in the post–World War II and Cold War technical workplace. Women computers at Langley and JPL forged their own career paths, frequently walking fine lines between their expected roles as wives and mothers and their desire to gain personal fulfillment through their careers.The computers’ experiences, however, were markedly different on the two sides of the country, particularly in terms of the racial and gender barriers they faced. Racial barriers were less overt at JPL, where women of multiple races and ethnicities worked in the same offices. In contrast, Langley was not integrated until the creation of NASA in 1958. Furthermore, at JPL, computer positions were not necessarily limited to women, whereas at Langley, computer positions were gender specific. But whether internally or externally enforced, at both locations women were pigeonholed into the role of computers, and they lacked advocates at management levels who might have made career advancement possible.Both authors make excellent use of primary sources, including oral histories, NASA documents, and newspaper articles. When scholarly works are cited, however, it appears they are only used for technical information. In drawing back the curtain on their stories, neither Shetterly nor Holt takes advantage of the significant work by scholars of race and gender studies; doing so would have bolstered their narratives.Shetterly and Holt also do not dig to the level of internal NASA policy, as Margaret Weitekamp did with her research on female pilots tested for astronaut training in Right Stuff, Wrong Sex: America’s First Women in Space Program (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2004), or relate the experiences of the female computers to the challenges faced by nonwhite males working at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, as Richard Paul and Steven Moss do in their book We Could Not Fail: The First African Americans in the Space Program (University of Texas Press, 2015). Shetterly and Holt, unfortunately, miss the opportunity to use their stories to investigate bigger questions about the perception of and reaction to race and gender at NASA or movements for racial and gender equality.As a woman historian, it was impossible not to feel thrilled and enlightened by the women in Hidden Figures and Rise of the Rocket Girls. Katherine Johnson, a passionate and talented mathematician whom Shetterly profiles, persisted in overcoming preconceptions of what women could contribute to human spaceflight. Susan Finley, a major figure in Holt’s book, continues to shape planetary exploration projects at JPL and inspires women professionals at the lab despite her lack of formal education.Unfortunately, both authors tend to jump from personal to professional stories, and the sudden topic changes can be confusing and difficult to follow. Shetterly also does not distinguish clearly between the experiences of the characters she profiles and those of other women at Langley. Admittedly, telling the story of all women at Langley was not one of Shetterly’s goals, but the reader might wonder how common or uncommon the experiences of Johnson and the others were.For narratives built on such a large number of oral histories, it was surprising not to hear more from other employees at NASA, particularly the engineers who supervised the women. The voices of those who benefited from their work would have added depth to the authors’ descriptions of the NASA work environments. Women mathematicians and engineers at Langley and JPL faced incredible odds in pursuing personal and professional goals simultaneously, but I never got a sense of what either set of women meant to the programs for which they worked. What is quite apparent is the remarkable strength of the communities the women built to support each other inside and outside the workplace.Although neither Holt nor Shetterly engages with the breadth of existing scholarship on race and gender issues at NASA or its predecessors, they forge new pathways for additional investigations. Taking a multibiographical approach does complicate their narratives, but those complications are necessary to relate the stories. The female technical experts, well aware of their uniqueness in their fields and in their places of employment, played important roles in human and robotic spaceflight, despite decades of being hidden from public view. Uncovering and telling such stories will hopefully lead to deeper scholarly examinations that will enrich our understanding of what women of all backgrounds meant to NASA and what NASA continues to mean to young women interested in careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.© 2017 American Institute of Physics.

title: Medical education in low- and middle-income countries must be innovated without neglecting its foundational principles
abstract: In 2019, national health workforces lacked at least 6•4 million physicians, with the largest shortage in low-income settings (1). Medical schools in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) need to be rethought and adapted to the needs of society and to a changing environment. This very difficult task must be accomplished if we wish to have good physicians and surgeons who will be able to diagnose and treat the population of those countries in the years to come. To reach this essential objective, public medical schools are of paramount importance, and their mission cannot be accomplished unless ministries of health are fully onboard and able to guarantee proper working conditions and career paths for newly graduated doctors. Adequate healthcare services and salaries of healthcare workers in the public sector are very important (2) to solve the issue of the export of medical doctors from LMICs that have invested in their training to high-income countries.How can medical schools in LMICs (many of which currently have huge problems and deficiencies) (3) be up to the challenge?Medical schools must graduate competent and compassionate physicians who are up to date with current trends in medicine. They must be able to help prevent diseases, to diagnose and treat sick people, to understand research data and its limits, and to mentor medical students and residents.The ministries of health must have a leading role in planning the minimum number of medical graduates needed in the following five-ten years, and the minimum and maximum number of students who should be enrolled in each medical school. Nowadays medical schools, following the example of Western ones, are obsessed with publicizing their admissions rankings, graduation rates, faculties' achievements and number of publications. These statistics are considered essential to foster accountability and improvement. However, as written by Jerry Z. Muller in his book about higher education, The Tyranny of Metrics, an "excellent method to increase graduation rates is to lower the standards for graduation" and demonstrating the accountability of a school through its excellent metric of performance; "the fact that no one has learned much, is beside the point"(4). This attitude must be avoided at all costs by any medical school, where the traditional reliance on experiential professional judgment must not be superseded by metric-driven assessments of comparative performance. Visibility must not be privileged over substance.It is time for medical schools not to seek accreditations based on enormous compliance paperwork that may not reflect their reality but rather concentrate on making sure that their graduates are truly competent, based on competent and experienced faculty and on serious assessments. The purpose of any public medical schools in LMICs must be to graduate practicing doctors able to serve their own countries, not to prepare their graduates to do their residencies and then work in high-income countries. This is extremely important, as each country must consider what their peculiarities are and which aspects the medical curriculum must particularly focus on.The medical curriculum in any LMIC must meet the needs of the population of the country where the medical school is located. Planning is essential to avoid content overload, that leads to students' surface learning and rote memorization rather than proper understanding. To integrate basic with clinical sciences, to make students understand their relevance, to promote deep learning, to learn communication, collaboration, respect, leadership and to encourage self-directed learning are all ambitious goals of any curriculum in whatever medical school nowadays. However, this easy rhetoric must be abandoned to look at the difficult practice, i.e. whether a theoretically attractive curriculum is indeed able to produce competent doctors.Two main issues must be considered when planning a curriculum. The first is today's concerning drive towards an unrealistic degree of "completeness" within an often-reduced timeframe. We live in an era of big data, predictive analytics, new medical devices, robotics and artificial intelligence (AI), where the art of medicine is considered obsolete, and physicians are being increasingly and erroneously moved away from direct patient contact. The second issue is the facilitation of transition from medical school to practice; in fact, most newly graduated physicians struggle more because they were not taught how to think clearly under real, stressful clinical pressure than because of lack of knowledge (5,6).In Western countries, assessments of learning can be divided into non-clinically-based, done in simulated clinical environments, and clinically-based (7). Six domains of competence are supposedly assessed: patient care, medical knowledge, professionalism, interpersonal and communication skills, practice-based learning and improvement, and systems-based practice (8).In LMICs, wWe need to make sure that medical students in LMICs know all the essentials; hence, the curriculum must promote clinical reasoning, observational skills (visual symptoms of illness or injury), critical thinking, and must provide sufficient self-study time. Surgical, medical, obstetrical procedures and ultrasound need to be learned and practiced by any individual student. The threshold to pass any assessments must not be low, and if students fail exams, they should re-take them. In addition, in an era where cheating is increasingly common (7,8,9,10,11,12), In addition, in an era where cheating is increasingly common (7,8,9,10), the role of oral exams, largely used in the past, must not be overlooked, if we want to make sure that medical school exams should be largely oral, as they used to be in the past, to allow the assessment of both students' knowledge and critical thinking are assessed (13,14,15,16). The rhetoric of the risk that oral exams are influenced by lecturers' personal knowledge of the students and by their subjective opinion must be abandoned, as structured oral examination has shown high levels of validity and reliability (17).. Without oral exams and serious assessment of student learning, based also on oral exams, graduation cannot serve as evidence of learning.Equity in healthcare must be learned and practiced. Students should help to provide care for vulnerable people (with well-defined competencies), and any public medical school should be committed to improving performance at a certain level of care (e.g., primary care) in a poor district/area of a city, or in villages.The curriculum must be organized in such a way that research is understood, and students are able to write during their clinical years (under supervision) case reports to be submitted for publication; this writing would reinforce the notion that reaching a reasonably sure diagnosis requirerequires appropriate investigation.Finally, it must be considered that internship is an essential and very important training period (18). In LMICs, it should not be an extra one or two years after graduationmedical school but should rather be incorporated in the curriculum for medical schools to be able to control how well internship is done and whether supervision is present and appropriate. Too often those interns who do their internship after graduation to be allowed to practice independently are currently regarded in many instances as a much-needed extra pair of hands in a disorganized environment rather than doctors under probation still requiring supervision and training.Public medical schools should recruit the brightest clinicians in their countries and very good doctors from other countries. To succeed in this, meritocracy must be real and not just formal in both enrolment and subsequent promotion decisions.Nowadays stakeholders' demand for measurable outcomes (e.g., graduate employability, number of publications and of their citations, presumed teaching quality, financial efficiency) has led to data-driven management, KPIs, and outcome-based funding of universities, similarly to corporate governance. Collegial governance has been replaced by managerialism and faculty autonomy is increasingly limited. With medical schools' reputation influenced by rankings in national and international league tables, the requirement for high numbers of largely irrelevant publications has led to a discouragement of long-term or high-risk projects, and to favoring safe, fashionable, shortterm ones (191). Time to prepare for teaching and to teach has progressively decreased, with negative consequences on the development of students able to reflect and think critically. It is also dangerous recruiting or promoting professors with very limited clinical experience who got their titles based on number (rather than relevance) of publications and not on teaching and patient care.LMICs must invest seriously in medical schools and in faculty quality. Teaching must be highly respected, well paid and well-supported. The relative importance of clinical commitment, teaching and research to recruitment and career progression (currently often unbalanced towards "research" consisting of publications) must be modified. As for research, a medical school in LMIC must not chase publications but try, if not to make new, significant discoveries, at least to contribute and find solutions to medical issues relevant to its own country and population.Finally, education in a medical school must be at a university level, i.e. must integrate teaching with clinical experience, reflection and a critical understanding of recent findings. Teaching cannot be delivered by anyone in any subject. Permanent academic staff is therefore essential and must be commensurate withto the student numbers; hiring inexperienced staff on short-term contracts can only eventually be a temporary solution. Having faculty with insufficient or no direct clinical and/or research experience in the taught subject/field who ask AI to make slides and read them, makes a bad medical school.The issue of AI is extremely important in nowadays medical education. Overreliance on it, with acceptance of AI-generated recommendations without question, affects the students' critical cognitive capabilities, including decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning (2012). The curriculum must allow students to develop self-awareness of AI usage and help prevent excessive dependence on it and on mobile technology (2113); critical thinking must be promoted and passive reliance on AI tools must be strongly discouraged. Hence, the contribution of psychologists and technology experts to curriculum design is essential. AI has completely changed the process of intellectual maturity forming through engagement with difficulty, cohering and repetition that progressively improve judgment; automatic responses to questions and automatically summarized literature have made the labor of cognition, that previously required hours of reading and revising, disappear (2214). The risk of surface-level synthesis and cognitive dependency is very high, whereas learning should be an active conversation between machine output and human understanding.To start using AI as rapidly and largely as possible in medical schools and/or in healthcare is a mistake; students and doctors should rather stay up to date on AI and thoughtfully introduce and apply it.An evidence-informed and consensus-guided framework can help in enabling medical schools to better prepare their future physicians for the digital transformation in health care (2315). Obviously, medical schools in LMICs should judiciously adapt this framework to their needs and resources.We live in an era of great difficulty for medical doctors worldwide. Seeing patients dying and then being blamed for it, getting litigation threats from patients and their relatives, being publicly criticized as "killers" on social media, newspapers and televisions leads good and experienced doctors to leave the profession. Young doctors learn not to take high-risk cases, defensive medicine increases (2416), and the whole medical environment becomes unattractive. It is therefore essential to select students very carefully through the right selection process (25,2617,18). Importantly, enrolling in a medical school must not mean a guarantee of success or of getting a medical degree without being competent. The shortage of doctors in any country must not translate into graduating any medical student, even if unprepared and unfit for the profession (27).Public medical schools need bold and innovative leaders who steer their institutions towards genuine scholarship and are conscious of the huge importance for any LMIC of having good and competent doctors. Being innovative implies not only to knowknowing and utilizinge new developments, but also not to being afraid to take initiatives against mainstream, and not to passively following current Western ideas about how a medical school must operate and about how teaching and assessments (28,2919,20) must be done. Faculty must not be expected to take huge extra lecture loads, teach multiple subjects outside their area of specialization, have assigned lengthy accreditation files, or have heavy non-academic work; they must be academics, not multitasking administrators. In fact, inadequate salaries and high non-academic workload cause demotivation, rote teaching, poor and non-innovative research. It is obviously important that each public medical school adapts to the culture of the country where it is located; however, this adaptation must not compromise the quality, skills and competence of the newly graduated doctors. Finally, it is very important not to follow private medical schools in focusing heavily on internet visibility, with dedicated management of Instagram reels, LinkedIn posts, Facebook pages, and YouTube content showcasing all kinds of events and supposed achievements. Faculty and students must concentrate on teaching and learning rather than coordinating likes, shares, and engagement. The reputation of a medical school must be based on the validity of the physicians that come out of it, not on perception in reputation surveys for all kindkinds of rankings.

title: Round up
abstract: OLAPARIB WITHOUT ANDROGEN DEPRIVATION FOR HIGH-RISK BIOCHEMICALLY RECURRENT PROSTATE CANCER FOLLOWING RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY: A NONRANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL This phase 2, single-arm, nonrandomized controlled trial enrolled genetically unselected patients who had biochemical recurrence (BCR) following radical prostatectomy (RP), a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) doubling time of 6 months or shorter, an absolute PSA value of 1.0 ng/mL or higher, and a testosterone level of 150 ng/dL or higher.[1] Olaparib was given at a dose of 300 mg orally, twice daily. It was continued until doubling of the baseline PSA, clinical or radiographic progression, or on development of unacceptable toxic effects. The primary endpoint was a confirmed 50% or higher decline in PSA from the baseline (PSA50). The secondary endpoints were the outcomes by homologous recombination repeat (HRR) alteration status, safety, and tolerability. Of the 51 patients enrolled, 13 participants (26%) had a PSA50 response, all within the HRR-positive group (13 of 27 participants [48%]). All 11 participants with BRCA2 alterations experienced a PSA50 response. Olaparib monotherapy led to high and durable PSA50 response rates in patients with BRCA2 alterations. Olaparib can be used as a treatment strategy for select patients with BCR following RP but does not have sufficient activity in those without HRR alterations. IMPACT OF COMPLETE TRANSURETHRAL RESECTION ON OUTCOMES IN PATIENTS RECEIVING RADIOTHERAPY FOR MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER TUMOR Nonmetastatic bladder cancer patients with cT2-4a and cN0-2 underwent radiotherapy (RT) with curative intent from 2002 to 2018.[2] All patients included in the study underwent bladder sparing, because they either refused RC, or were considered surgically unfit. The extent of transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) was derived from the operative report and was classified based on the surgeon’s description as visibly complete or incomplete. Following TURBT, curative-intent RT was delivered either alone or with concurrent chemotherapy (trimodal therapy) preceded or not by neo-adjuvant chemotherapy. Complete response (CR) was defined as the absence of residual bladder cancer on posttreatment TURBT and locoregional disease on cross-sectional imaging. Of the 757 patients included, 66% (498) had documentation of a complete and 34% (259) an incomplete TURBT. The adjusted median follow-up was 27 months. Adjusted survival analyses showed no significant difference in a 5-year overall survival (48% vs. 52%, 1.03 [0.82–1.29]; P = 0.8), cancer-specific survival (64% vs. 61%, 0.93 [0.70–1.25]; P = 0.7), metastasis-free survival (43% vs. 46%, 0.97 [0.79–1.19]; P = 0.8), and disease-free survival (32% vs. 35%, 0.95 [0.79–1.15]; P = 0.7) between the two groups. In this large, multi-institutional cohort of patients undergoing curative-intent RT for MIBC, complete TURBT before RT was not associated with improved CR or survival outcomes. The extent of TURBT was not independently associated with oncologic outcomes in patients with MIBC treated with radiation therapy. QUALITY-OF-LIFE OUTCOMES OF THE ROBOTIC-ASSISTED VERSUS CONVENTIONAL OPEN PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY II TRIAL The ROBOtic-assisted versus conventional open partial nephrectomy II trial was a randomized controlled feasibility trial comparing robot-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) and open partial nephrectomy (OPN) in terms of health-related quality of life (HRQoL).[3] Conducted at the University Medical Center Mannheim, the study involved 50 patients and assessed various HRQoL metrics through validated questionnaires (Kidney Disease Quality of Life-Short Form, Quality of Life Questionnaire C30, computerized adaptive testing EORTC QLQ-C30, the EuroQoL five Dimensions five Levels questionnaire, convalescence and recovery evaluation score questionnaire) at baseline, hospital discharge, and postoperatively at 30 and 90 days. The results showed that RAPN was associated with significantly lower pain scores and better outcomes in physical functioning and gastrointestinal symptoms compared to OPN at hospital discharge and up to 30 days postoperatively. However, by 90 days, there were no significant differences between the two approaches. The study highlights RAPN’s short-term benefits in clinically significant pain management and suggests the need for further research into the long-term outcomes. EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF VIBEGRON FOR PERSISTENT SYMPTOMS OF OVERACTIVE BLADDER IN MEN BEING PHARMACOLOGICALLY TREATED FOR BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA: RESULTS FROM THE PHASE 3 RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED COURAGE TRIAL The phase 3 COURAGE trial assessed Vibegron, a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist, in men with Overactive Bladder (OAB) symptoms while receiving pharmacological treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).[4] This double-blind, placebo-controlled study included 1105 men who were randomized to receive either vibegron 75 mg or a placebo for 24 weeks. The trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of vibegron in improving OAB symptoms. Results showed that vibegron significantly reduced daily micturition frequency (−0.74 [−1.02–−0.46]; P < 0.0001) and urgency episodes (−0.95 [−1.37–−0.54]; P < 0.0001) compared to placebo. It also led to improvements in nocturia, urinary incontinence, and other symptoms. The treatment was well tolerated, with adverse event rates similar to placebo. The study demonstrated that vibegron is effective in reducing OAB symptoms in men already treated for BPH and has a favorable safety profile. RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY WITHOUT PRIOR BIOPSY IN PATIENTS EVALUATED BY 18F-LABELED PROSTATE-SPECIFIC MEMBRANE ANTIGEN LIGAND POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY/COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY AND MULTIPARAMETER MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING: A SINGLE-CENTER, PROSPECTIVE, SINGLE-ARM TRIAL This study investigated whether RP for localized Prostate Cancer (PCa) could be safely performed without a prior biopsy, using advanced imaging techniques instead.[5] The trial involved 47 patients who underwent both 18F-Labeled Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen Ligand Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography (18F-PSMA PET/CT) and multiparameter magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) before RP. These imaging methods, particularly when combined, demonstrated high accuracy in detecting clinically significant PCa (csPCa) and locating the index tumor (IT). The sensitivity and positive predictive value (PPV) for diagnosing PCa and csPCa were 71.3% and 91.9% and 88.9% and 90.3%, respectively. All the patients were diagnosed with csPCa on final histopathology, and the IT was accurately localized in 95.7% of the cases. The study showed that RP without biopsy is feasible, with no increase in positive surgical margins compared to traditional methods. Despite some limitations, such as the small sample size and short follow-up, the study supports the potential for biopsy-free RP using advanced imaging tools to enhance the diagnosis and surgical outcomes. MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING AND PROSTATE-SPECIFIC MEMBRANE ANTIGEN-POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY FOR PREDICTION OF EXTRA PROSTATIC EXTENSION OF PROSTATE CANCER This prospective, pilot, single-arm trial included patients with intermediate or high-risk PCa as per National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines who elected RP.[6] The primary objective was to compare the sensitivity and specificity of mpMRI and PSMA-PET for predicting posterior extra prostatic extension (EPE) at nerve bundles. The secondary objectives included assessing imaging accuracy for seminal vesicle involvement (SVI) and pelvic lymph node involvement. After mpMRI and PSMA-PET images were read for EPE prediction, surgeons prospectively answered questionnaires based on mpMRI and PSMA-PET scans on the decision for nerve-sparing or non-nerve-sparing approach. Final whole-mount pathology was the reference standard. PSMA-PET showed higher sensitivity for EPE than mpMRI (0.87 vs. 0.57, P = 0.03), with similar specificity (0.77 vs. 0.73, P = 0.49). In favorable intermediate risk cases, false-positive rates were similar, but PSMA-PET had significantly higher sensitivity in unfavorable intermediate-risk cases. mpMRI had better sensitivity for SVI detection (P = 0.03), while PSMA-PET was better for lymph node involvement (P = 0.05). PSMA-PET correctly identified 20 out of 27 nerve bundles compared to 7 for mpMRI. Surgeons’ nerve-sparing predictions were more accurate with PSMA-PET and mpMRI (74%) versus mpMRI alone (65%). The authors concluded that PSMA-PET combined with mpMRI improved surgical decision making for nerve-sparing RP by enhancing sensitivity for EPE and lymph node involvement, while mpMRI remained superior for detecting SVI. RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL COMPARING OPEN SIMPLE PROSTATECTOMY OR PROSTATE ARTERY EMBOLIZATION IN LARGE PROSTATES This single-center, randomized controlled trial was designed to test the noninferiority of prostate artery embolization (PAE) compared to open simple prostatectomy (OP) in patients with large prostates (>80 mL).[7] The primary endpoint was the change in peak flow rate (Qmax) at 6 months. The co-primary endpoints were changes in detrusor pressure at maximum flow (PdetQmax) and bladder outlet obstruction index (BOOI) at 6 months. There was a significant difference in Qmax change between the OP and PAE groups, favoring the OP group. PdetQmax and BOOI change also significantly favored the OP group. However, PAE had a significantly shorter hospital stay and lower blood transfusion requirements. Postoperative perineal discomfort and LUTS as measured by visual analogue scale (VAS) scores were significantly higher in the PAE group. No significant difference was observed in IPSS score changes between the two groups. The authors concluded that PAE was inferior to open prostatectomy in improving urinary flow and reducing bladder outlet obstruction. However, PAE offered the benefit of significantly shorter hospital stays. PROPHYLACTIC USE OF BIOLOGIC MESH IN ILEAL CONDUIT: A RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL This randomized controlled trial investigated the impact of prophylactic biologic mesh on preventing parastomal hernia (PSH) in patients undergoing cystectomy with ileal conduit (IC).[8] Conducted at the University of Southern California, the study included 146 patients randomized to receive either FlexHD biologic mesh using a sublay intraperitoneal technique or standard IC without mesh. Patients were monitored through physical examinations and CT scans for up to 2 years. The primary endpoint was the time to radiological PSH, whereas secondary outcomes included clinical PSH and mesh-related complications. The results showed no significant difference in PSH incidence between the mesh and control groups. Radiological PSH occurred in 37 patients (18 with mesh vs. 19 controls) and clinical PSH was observed in 16 patients (8 in each group). The study found no significant protective effect of the mesh, with similar PSH-free survival rates at 1 and 2 years. In addition, no mesh-related adverse events were reported. The study concluded that while the use of biologic mesh is safe, it does not significantly reduce the risk of PSH within 2 years after surgery. Financial support and sponsorship: Nil. Conflicts of interest: There are no conflicts of interest.

title: Euro-Chinese consensus on accessory cavitated uterine malformation
abstract: Accessory cavitated uterine malformation (ACUM) is a rare obstructive uterine anomaly that remains poorly understood, posing challenges for clinical management. The aetiopathogenesis is hypothesised to involve the duplication and persistence of ductal Müllerian tissue usually near the round ligament attachment, potentially related to gubernaculum dysfunction. ACUM is specifically classified by Acién’s system, though rare variants necessitate continued international research to refine classification frameworks. This consensus aims to develop good clinical practice recommendations for the pathophysiology, terminology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of ACUM. A working group consisted of Chinese and European experts, after approval from the European Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy, developed recommendations based on the best available evidence and experts’ opinion. Patients with ACUM present with typical symptoms such as dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia, and atypical symptoms, including gastrointestinal and generalized pelvic pain. Diagnostic criteria include isolated cavitated lesions in the anterolateral myometrium near the round ligament, lined by endometrial tissue and filled with haemorrhagic fluid, surrounded by a myometrial mantle with concentric orientation of myometrial fibres, and typically associated with a normal uterine cavity. Diagnosis is most accurately made through ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging. Surgical excision of the ACUM is considered the definitive treatment offering near-complete symptom resolution, and a minimally invasive approach should be preferred when possible. The timing of surgery and the interval before attempting pregnancy remain unclear. The mode of delivery post-surgery is individualised based on the degree of myometrial involvement. The current consensus summarises the existing evidence on ACUM, providing good clinical practice recommendations for its management. Existing gaps in the understanding and management of ACUMs, highlight the need for further research to guide clinical decision-making. The key points of the consensus are summarized below. For the full content, please refer to the supplementary file, https://links.lww.com/CM9/C525. Part I: Embryology of the Internal Genitalia Key question: What are the current theories on the etiopathogenesis of ACUM? Key point: ACUMs could be caused by the duplication and persistence of ductal Müllerian tissue in the critical area at the attachment level of the round ligament, possibly related to a gubernaculum dysfunction or abnormal traction.[1,2] Key question: What is the most appropriate terminology for accessory cavitated uterine malformation? Key point: Accessory cavitated uterine malformation (ACUM) is the preferred terminology. Key question: How is accessory cavitated uterine malformation classified according to the existing classification systems? Key points: (1) Acién’s classification is the only system which specifically refers to the ACUM.[3] (2) Clinicians who care for patients with Müllerian anomalies should be mindful of existence of other rare, unique and potentially very complex variants. (3) Continued international efforts are needed to conduct high-quality studies that offer evidence-based data to improve the classification systems and their applicability in clinical practice. Part II: Clinical Presentation, Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis Key question: What are the typical and atypical symptoms in patients with ACUM? Key points: (1) Typical symptoms: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and recurrent pelvic pain. (2) Atypical symptoms: gastrointestinal pain and generalised pelvic pain as can be seen in any chronic/recurrent pain problem. (3) ACUMs should be considered in all young women presenting with severe menstrual pain symptoms after menarche. Key question: What are the diagnostic criteria for an ACUM? Key points: In order to diagnose ACUM, the following criteria should be fulfilled: (1) An isolated cavitated lesion located in the anterolateral myometrium, in the proximity of the round ligament. (2) The cavity is lined by endometrial tissue and typically filled with haemorrhagic/menstrual fluid. (3) The cavity is surrounded by a myometrial mantle with concentric orientation of myometrial fibres. (4) They are typically associated with a normal uterine cavity. Additional notes: While large ACUMs may enlarge to involve the posterolateral myometrium, because they are thought to originate from the gubernaculum. They should predominantly be within the anterolateral myometrium. ACUMs are found within the myometrium but the extent of their involvement with the myometrium can vary. They can be completely embedded within the myometrium or substantially outside the myometrium with minimal myometrial involvement. A grading system could be used to describe this based on the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) classification of type 4, type 5 and type 6 fibroids as this will inform the extent of surgical dissection necessary as well as the risk of uterine cavity breach. Key question: What are the diagnostic tools for diagnosing accessory cavitated uterine malformation? Key points: (1) In expert hands, the diagnosis of ACUM can confidently be made on transvaginal or transrectal ultrasound.[4] (2) If there is diagnostic uncertainty after ultrasound examination, consideration should be given to using MRI. (3) Not all histopathologists are familiar with ACUMs so it is important to let them know that you suspect an ACUM and ensure they are aware of their histopathological features. Differential diagnoses: The main differential diagnoses of ACUM are listed in Table 1. Table 1 - Features of accessory congenital uterine malformations and relevant differential diagnoses. Items Accessory cavitated uterine malformations Cystic adenomyomas Rudimentary horn with functioning endometrial cavity Complete septate uterus with unilateral cervical aplasia (Robert uterus) Degenerated fibroids Location Located in the anterolateral myometrium, in proximity to the round ligament Located in the myometrium Located at the lateral cornual aspect or lateral and distinct to the myometrium Located in the lateral aspect of the uterus with a thin septum between cavities that can be bulging Can be located anywhere in the myometrium Pathophysiology Having a myometrial mantle and endometrial lining Absence of myometrial mantle No myometrial mantle Will not have a myometrial mantle that is distinct from surrounding myometrium Fibroid pseudo capsule and heterogeneous aspect Relation to the uterine corpus Typically bulge outside the uterine corpus Typically entirely within the myometrium Can be separated from the main uterine body or not, but the uterine cavity will be unicornuate. Typically within the uterine corpus Could be within the body of the uterus or pedunculated Content Typically echogenic cavity content Often anechoic cavity content There is usually not hematometra found because the content refluxes into the abdomen Typically echogenic content Can be echogenic or anechoic content Age Commonly found in young women or teenagers Commonly found in older parous women Can be found in any age group Commonly found in young women or teenagers Can be found in any age group Key point: As exclusion of other uterine anomalies is crucial to the diagnosis, in the rare circumstances where ultrasound and MRI have failed to clarify the morphology of the uterine cavity, consideration could be given to more invasive tests such as saline infusion sonohysterography, Hysterosalpingo-Contrast Sonography/Hysterosalpingo-Foam Sonography or hysteroscopy. Part III: Treatment and Counselling Key question: What are the clinical indications and available treatment options for ACUM? Key points: (1) Treatment aims to restore uterine anatomy through excision of the ACUM and to alleviate symptoms. (2) ACUM typically requires treatment in case of severe dysmenorrhea or chronic/recurrent pelvic pain. (3) Surgical management, consisting of ACUM removal from the myometrium and suturing of the uterine defect, is the definitive treatment and it has shown nearly complete remission of symptoms. Options include laparotomy, laparoscopy, and robot-assisted laparoscopy. A minimally invasive approach should be preferred when possible.[5] (4) Medical management including administration of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs, Oral Contraceptive Pill, Levonorgestrel-Releasing IntraUterine System, and Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone agonists; Medical management provides temporary relief but is often not a definitive solution. (5) Sclerotherapy is an alternative for those who wish to avoid surgery, though it may lead to recurrence. Key question: What are the optimal skills and facilities to remove the ACUM while protecting the uterine myometrium wall? Key points: (1) Ability to accurately estimate the penetration depth in the myometrium to remove the lesion while minimizing risks. (2) Use of intraoperative ultrasound, including 3D ultrasonography, for precise localization and excision of the ACUM. (3) Surgical skills and experience to apply proper surgical techniques including careful enucleation of the ACUM using mechanical, monopolar or bipolar energy, with various tools assisting in the dissection and suturing (especially for laparoscopy/robotics) Key question: What is the best timing of surgery for ACUM? Key point: There is no direct evidence to guide the timing of ACUM surgery. Key question: What is the recommended interval before attempting pregnancy after surgery? Key point: After surgery for ACUM, a recommended waiting period of 4–6 months is advised before attempting pregnancy; this allows the proper healing of the myometrium. Key question: What is the recommended mode of delivery for future pregnancy? Key point: There are no data to determine the optimal mode of delivery after ACUM excision; Caesarean sections and vaginal deliveries are described in literature. In determining the mode of delivery after ACUM excision, consideration should be given to the depth of myometrial involvement/FIGO type of ACUM. In conclusion, there remains a great deal that is unknown about ACUMs, which provides challenges for clinicians managing patients with this malformation. The embryological origin remains unclear although it is possibly related to a gubernaculum dysfunction or abnormal traction. Existing classification systems except for Acién’s, while widely utilised, do not adequately incorporate ACUM. To diagnose an ACUM, the following criteria should be fulfilled: to be an isolated cavitated lesion located in the anterolateral myometrium, in the proximity of the round ligament with a cavity lined by endometrial tissue and typically filled with haemorrhagic/menstrual fluid. They should be surrounded by a myometrial mantle with typical concentric orientation of the myometrial fibres with a normal uterine cavity. Current management strategies prioritise complete surgical excision of the lesion, preferably via minimally invasive techniques, to achieve symptom resolution. There is a paucity of high-quality evidence to guide clinical decision-making regarding aspects of optimal surgical intervention and more specifically regarding the management of future pregnancies. Funding This work was supported by grants from the National Key Clinical Specialty Construction Project (No. U114000) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 82271656). Conflicts of Interest None.

title: SHOP TALK: New Jobs, Appointments, & Changes; Promotions; Honors; Grants, & Other ‘People News’
abstract: SHOP TALKWILLIAM PAO, MD, PHDWilliam Pao, MD, PhD, Associate Professor of Medicine and Director of Personalized Cancer Medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, has been named Director of the Division of Hematology and Oncology in the Department of Medicine, a position that took effect on October 5. “Dr. Pao has demonstrated tremendous leadership and creativity since arriving at Vanderbilt,” said Nancy J. Brown, MD, Chair and Physician-in-Chief of the Department of Medicine. “Dr. Pao's depth of experience as a translational scientist, his commitment to excellence in patient care, and his commitment to developing people and programs made him the ideal choice for this post.” As a fellow working in the laboratory of now NCI Director Harold Varmus, MD, Dr. Pao first identified EGF receptor mutations that convey sensitivity to gefitinib and erlotinib in lung cancers in non-smokers, a landmark work that has been cited some 1,440 times since its publication in 2004. Dr. Pao is also the co-founder, with Mia Levy, MD, of MyCancerGenome, an online tool to enable a genetically informed approach to cancer medicine. This year's European Society for Medical Oncology awards were as follows:PROF JOHANN DE BONOPROF RAFAEL ROSELLPROF HANS JÖRG SENN The ESMO Award, to Prof Johann de Bono of the Institute of Cancer Research of the Royal Marsden Hospital, for outstanding contributions in translational and clinical research, innovative treatment, education, and development of international guidelines for prostate cancer management. The Hamilton Fairley Award, to Prof Rafael Rosell of Catalan Institute of Oncology in Badalona, Spain, who established a leading center in lung cancer treatment at Hospital Trias i Pujol. The award commemorates one of the founding fathers of medical oncology in Europe and is presented to candidates who are internationally recognized for lifetime achievements in science and clinical/laboratory research. The ESMO Lifetime Achievement Award, Prof Hans Jörg Senn of the Tumor and Breast Centre ZeTuP in St Gallen, Switzerland, recognized for his work in organizing educational activities that set the standards of care in breast cancer, especially adjuvant treatment, as well as bringing prevention strategies to medical oncologists in Europe. “His outstanding efforts through the organization of Consensus Conferences among breast cancer experts focused attention on addressing subtle questions in the adjuvant treatment of breast cancer, which presented a dilemma for practicing physicians,” said Prof Franco Cavalli, Chair of the ESMO Lifetime Achievement Award Committee. ARMANDO GIULIANO – OKArmando E. Giuliano, MD, and Carlos L. Arteaga, MD, will receive this year's Susan G. Komen for the Cure Brinker Awards for Scientific Distinction. The awards will be given at the CTRC-AACR San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium in December.CARLOS ARTEAGA, MDDr. Giuliano is Executive Vice Chair of Surgery for Surgical Oncology at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles; and Dr. Arteaga is Professor of Medicine and Cancer Biology at Vanderbilt University. Dr. Giuliano is receiving the Brinker Award for Scientific Distinction in Clinical Research for research that has led to less invasive surgical treatments for breast cancer, specifically the removal of fewer lymph nodes in certain women with early stage breast cancer. Dr. Arteaga is receiving the Brinker Award for Scientific Distinction in Basic Science for his work explaining the role of key proteins and growth factor receptors in the pathogenesis of breast cancer, providing the basis for targeted therapies. Drs. Giuliano and Arteaga will deliver keynote lectures at the conference, and their institutions will each also receive a $25,000 award to further their activities in breast cancer research.DOUGLAS E. PETERSON, DMD, PHDDouglas E. Peterson, DMD, PhD, has received the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh's “Award of Fellowship in Dental Surgery Without Examination,” one of the college's highest international honors. Dr. Peterson, Professor of Oral Medicine in the Department of Oral Health and Diagnostic Sciences at the University of Connecticut and Head of the Carole and Ray Neag Comprehensive Cancer Center's Head and Neck Cancer/Oral Oncology Program, received the award during the college's diploma ceremony last month in Edinburgh.JAMES P. ALLISON, PHDThe Cancer Research Institute (CRI) has named James P. Allison, PhD, as the new Director of the Scientific Advisory Council, succeeding founding scientific and medical director Lloyd J. Old, MD, who served in that role for 40 years. Dr. Allison is David H. Koch Chair in Immunological Studies and Chair of the Immunology Program at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center and creator of ipilimumab. “Jim Allison's stature within the immunology, cancer immunology, and general scientific communities is nearly unrivaled,” Dr. Old said in a statement. “Moreover, Jim has a strong personal commitment to developing better and safer treatments for cancer patients, and a proven track record in bringing a basic discovery from the laboratory into a successful treatment for patients. We are confident that he is the ideal person to direct CRI's strategic priorities and growth in the years ahead.” In addition, CRI gave this year's William B. Coley Award for Distinguished Research in Tumor Immunology jointly to Philip D. Greenberg, MD, Professor of Medicine and Immunology at the University of Washington School of Medicine and Head of the Program in Immunology at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center; and Steven A. Rosenberg, MD, PhD, Chief of Surgery at the National Cancer Institute and Professor of Surgery at the Uniformed Services University of Health Sciences and George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences. The award was given in recognition for their pioneering work to bring adoptive T cell therapy from its experimental foundations in the laboratory, through proof of concept, to its successful application in the clinic as a treatment for cancer. The award was given at the organization's 25th Annual Awards Dinner, held October 3 in New York City. Also presented at the CRI dinner was the Frederick W. Alt Award for New Discoveries in Immunology, given to Stephen C. Jameson, PhD, a former CRI postdoctoral fellowship recipient whose work has shed important light on the mechanisms of T cell activation and differentiation; the Oliver R. Grace Award for Distinguished Service in Advancing Cancer Research, given to Mitchell H. Gold, MD, President and CEO of Dendreon Corporation, and to film and television producer and Stand Up to Cancer Cofounder Laura Ziskin, who died earlier this year of metastatic breast cancer (OT, 6/25/11).CLARENCE H. “BUCK” BROWN III, MDClarence H. “Buck” Brown III, MD, has announced his retirement as President and CEO of MD Anderson Cancer Center Orlando at the end of next year, a position he has held since the institution started 20 years ago as the first outreach center of the University of Texas MD Anderson in Houston. Under Dr. Brown's leadership and guidance MD Anderson Orlando has grown to more than 50 full-time employed and 14 contracted physicians on staff and more than 420 employees, and the number of new patients seen each year has doubled, with approximately 5,000 new patients visiting the cancer center each year. Following his retirement, Dr. Brown will move into a new role with Orlando Health as President Emeritus of MD Anderson Orlando and Vice President of Development for the Orlando Health Foundation. Linda Meyer, RN, MSN, OCN, received the ASTRO Nurse Excellence Award, which is given annually to a registered nurse who is considered to go above and beyond the normal standards of nursing practice. She received the award, which includes a $1,000 grant, at the ASTRO Annual Meeting in Miami earlier this month. She is the radiation oncology nurse manager at Allegheny General Hospital in Pittsburgh, where she has worked since 1986, and manages the Radiation Oncology Network, which consists of seven facilities. She is also responsible for providing educational and training opportunities to nurses within the Radiation Oncology Network. She is also heavily involved in the Greater Pittsburgh Chapter of Oncology Nursing Society (ONS) and is the co-chairman of “Camp Raising Spirits,” a GPC-ONS project providing adult cancer patients with a weekend away.OLUFUNMILAYO FALUSI OLOPADE, MDOlufunmilayo Falusi Olopade, MD, was selected to deliver this year's AACR Distinguished Lecture on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities, funded by Susan G. Komen for the Cure. She is the Walter L. Palmer Distinguished Service Professor of Medicine and Human Genetics, and Associate Dean for Global Health at the University of Chicago Medical Center, and a member of the Komen Scholars scientific advisory panel. The lecture, “Closing the Knowledge Disparity Gap: From Molecular Mechanisms to Interventions and Back,” was delivered last month at the Fourth AACR Conference on The Science of Cancer Health Disparities. Kemp Kernstine, MD, PhD, has joined the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, as Chair of Thoracic Surgery. Dr. Kernstine, a pioneer in minimally invasive surgical techniques, designed many of the robotic chest surgery procedures in use today and teaches the techniques around the world. Prior to joining UT Southwestern, Dr. Kernstine was director of the lung cancer and thoracic oncology program at City of Hope Medical Center and Beckman Research Institute. Kimary Kulig, PhD, MPH, has joined the National Comprehensive Cancer Network as Vice President, Clinical & Translational Outcomes Research, where he will direct the development and advancement of the NCCN Oncology Outcomes Database. Prior to joining NCCN, Dr. Kulig worked for several years leading outcomes based research in oncology at Pfizer, Inc., most recently as Senior Director and Lead, Molecular Epidemiology Research, Oncology. The West Clinic in Memphis has started the Comprehensive Breast Center, a multidisciplinary breast center, which will be the first center of its kind in the region. The newly formed Comprehensive Breast Center at The West Clinic will partner with The Breast Clinic of Memphis and its breast surgical oncologist, Michael P. Berry, MD. Two additional breast surgeons from the area will also be joining the staff: Roy M. Oswaks, MD, and Russell H. Patterson, III, MD. The Cancer Therapy & Research Center at the University Health Science Center at San Antonio has started a new exercise center for cancer survivors, which is free and available to all cancer patients in the area, regardless of where they sought treatment. Patients can also bring close family members. Stacey Young-McCaughan, RN, PhD, AOCN, Professor in the Psychiatry Department of the School of Medicine, designed the program based on her 12 years of work with hundreds of cancer survivors at Brooke Army Medical Center. “It is so rewarding to see cancer survivors take back control of their lives with exercise, whether they are beginning again or just starting out,” Dr. Young-McCaughan said in a news release. “We do so many things to people with cancer, from drawing blood to administering treatments. This is something they can do for themselves, and people really appreciate that.” Survivors will receive complete physical assessments from the fitness center staff, who will design individualized fitness programs that participants can practice either at the facility or in their homes. They'll be asked to come in for further assessments, both to make sure they're doing well and give feedback to the staff, enabling the program to continue to produce more data on the links between cancer prevention and physical fitness. Over the next two years, the program is looking for 750 cancer survivors at any point along the cancer trajectory, and people interested in joining the study can call 210-450-1765. Funding is from the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas, with support from the School of Nursing and the Division of Behavioral Medicine at the Health Science Center. The Ohio Third Frontier Commission has awarded a $1 million research grant to advance the Philips Healthcare Global Advanced Imaging Innovation Center, a collaboration among Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals (UH) Case Medical Center, and Philips Healthcare. The funding will support a project to develop a first-of-its-kind system that will provide greatly enhanced resolution of PET to detect breast cancer through CT or MRI. Using the new PET/MRI at the UH Seidman Cancer Center, one of four in the world, researchers will explore if this hybrid imaging technology enhances the ability to more accurately detect breast cancer. Raymond Muzic, PhD, Associate Professor of Radiology, Oncology and Biomedical Engineering at Case Western Reserve University, is the overall project leader for the research team, which also includes Donna Plecha, MD;James O'Donnell, MD;Peter Faulhaber, MD; and Piotr Maniawski. Researchers at the University of Michigan Comprehensive Cancer Center have been awarded a $3.5 million grant from Susan G. Komen for the Cure to study cancer stem cells in triple-negative breast cancer. The grant is a collaboration with researchers at the Karmanos Cancer Institute in Detroit, the Van Andel Research Institute and the Translational Genomics Research Institute of Grand Rapids, Michigan, and Baylor College of Medicine in Houston. Among women with breast cancer, this subtype represents about 15% of diagnoses in Caucasian American women, 26% in African American women, and 82% in African women.MAX S. WICHA, MD“We urgently need to develop novel approaches to treat triple-negative breast cancer in order to reduce racial disparities. Through this Komen grant, we propose to develop novel therapies capable of attacking and destroying the lethal seeds driving these cancers, the cancer stem cells,” said Max S. Wicha, MD, Distinguished Professor of Oncology and Director of the Cancer Center. He and Patricia LoRusso, DO, Professor of Medicine at Karmanos, and Jeffrey Trent, PhD, President and Research Director at Van Andel and TGen, will be principal investigators. The Wistar Institute has broken ground on a major expansion—a seven-story, 89,700-square-foot research tower, which will rise above its current historic facility at 36th and Spruce streets in University City, Philadelphia. The project will enable Wistar to expand its research operations, recruit new scientific faculty, and pursue collaborative biomedical research in emerging areas of science. “At a time when biomedical research is advancing at a lightning pace, The Wistar Institute finds itself constrained by aging facilities designed for 19th and 20th century science,” said Wistar President and CEO Russel E. Kaufman, MD. “We designed our new building specifically to foster interactions between researchers in the kinds of multidisciplinary collaborations that spark innovation and drive results.” Tell Us!
